title: The Scraped Wall: Floresta, the Riachuelo, and the Perishable Record
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the birth
stops.date_confidence: year attested in the Spanish Wikipedia infobox and in Wikidata Q70874003; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01 January. A 2015 interview giving his age as forty-four would imply 1970 or 1971, unresolved.
stops.campa: A son is born in Buenos Aires in 1970, in a city whose walls are owned by advertising and by the paste-up men who work them at night. Nothing in the record marks the hospital or the street. He will be known across the country by a nickname long before he is known by his surname: Pelado, the bald one, a name a barrio hands out and an artist keeps. The walls he will spend his life scraping are already standing along the Riachuelo and the western avenues, grey, and he has not yet held a can.
suggested_refs: Wikidata Q70874003, birth statements for Alfredo Segatori
sources: Wikipedia (es), 'Alfredo Segatori', infobox
Wikidata Q70874003
Street Art Latam, 'Alfredo Segatori: el pionero que transformo el muralismo en Argentina'

stops.name: Floresta, three schools and a boy who will not sit
stops.date_confidence: approximate; the source gives no years for the school expulsions, only that they belong to his boyhood in Floresta. Floresta is attested as where he grew up, not as his birthplace.
stops.campa: He grows up in Floresta, in the working-class west of the city, and calls himself a man of the barrio before he calls himself anything else. Three schools expel him. He describes the boy he was as a vivo, a wise guy who cannot hold still for a classroom, whose attention goes out the window to the street and stays there. Floresta gives him the register he will paint in for thirty years: the neighborhood face, the corner kiosk, the flat afternoon light of a western avenue. It does not give him a single drawing lesson.
suggested_refs: The Floresta of the 1970s and 1980s, the barrio he names as his identity
sources: Diario Contexto, 'Alfredo Segatori y los colores de la identidad popular'

stops.name: Floresta, physical education and the sample case
stops.date_confidence: approximate; no source dates his studies or his early employment, and the date is a placeholder inside the years before the trade begins.
stops.campa: He studies Physical Education rather than art, and works as a gym teacher and then as a medical sales representative, carrying samples between clinics in a city that has no idea what he will do to its walls. He is self-taught in everything that will matter. From the late 1980s he is already painting walls, though the aerosol can that becomes his signature instrument is still a Brazilian tool he has never touched. No gallery knows his name and no newspaper prints it. The walls he learns on belong to whoever agreed to let him have them.
suggested_refs: The late-1980s wall work that precedes any aerosol, described in the trade press only as 'muralista urbano desde finales de los 80'
sources: Diario Contexto, 'Alfredo Segatori y los colores de la identidad popular'
arteforadomuseu.com.br, biography page for 'Pelado'
Street Art Latam profile

stops.name: Ibirapuera, Sao Paulo: the first aerosol
stops.date_confidence: sources disagree: Diario Contexto dates the Biennial trip to 1994, ojosalcuadro.tumblr.com dates his entry into street art to a 1996 Sao Paulo Biennial. Both are Biennial years and no third source adjudicates. Month and day unknown.
stops.campa: He travels north to the Bienal de Sao Paulo, into Ibirapuera Park, and meets Brazilian writers who have been working the largest city in the hemisphere with spray cans for years. They put one in his hand. It fights him. The spray does not feel like his medium, he says of that first attempt, and it will be a long time before the can obeys him the way a brush obeys. He comes home with a tool he cannot yet control and with the knowledge of what an entire city looks like once its writers have taken it.
suggested_refs: The Bienal de Sao Paulo pavilion in Ibirapuera Park, where he first handles an aerosol can
sources: Diario Contexto, 'Alfredo Segatori y los colores de la identidad popular'
ojosalcuadro.tumblr.com, 'Alfredo Segatori, un muralista de Buenos Aires' (2015)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, El Vomito Publicitario
stops.date_confidence: single-source reconstruction from a 2015 interview; no month, no day, and no address recorded anywhere.
stops.campa: Back from Brazil he paints his first Buenos Aires mural and calls it El Vomito Publicitario, the advertising vomit, aimed squarely at the paid images that own every surface in the city. He buys his own paint. Nobody pays him. He scrapes and primes the wall himself and then improvises straight onto it, no sketch, no plan, the colour decided in front of the brick. The method sets on that first wall and never changes: what other muralists work out on paper, he works out in public, at height, with the neighbors watching.
suggested_refs: 'El Vomito Publicitario', his first Buenos Aires mural, location unrecorded
sources: ojosalcuadro.tumblr.com, 'Alfredo Segatori, un muralista de Buenos Aires' (2015)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the press finds him
stops.date_confidence: approximate; the sources say only 'mediados de la decada de 1990' for the start of wider diffusion, with no exact year.
stops.campa: From the middle of the decade the newspapers begin printing his walls. He gives them a lineage when they ask for one: action painting, David Alfaro Siqueiros for the scale and for the politics of a wall that belongs to everybody, Jackson Pollock for the arm that decides before the mind does. He works freehand and refuses the projector and the grid. He prefers a rough wall to a smooth one, because a surface that has been weathered and patched takes paint the way skin takes weather.
suggested_refs: The action-painting lineage he claims: Siqueiros for scale, Pollock for the arm
sources: Wikipedia (es), 'Alfredo Segatori', citing Perfil, Cesar Calvo, 13 September 2019
Perfil, Cesar Calvo, 'La explosion de color en el puerto de Buenos Aires continua', 13 September 2019

stops.name: Centro Cultural Ricardo Rojas, the Aerosol Urbano course
stops.date_confidence: undated in the single source, which describes the course as ongoing; the date is an inference placed in his early teaching years.
stops.campa: On Avenida Corrientes, in the University of Buenos Aires cultural centre named for Ricardo Rojas, he teaches a course called Aerosol Urbano. What he passes on is not a style but a procedure: find a wall, ask for it, strip it, work it, and do not draw it first. Students leave the classroom and paint the city themselves. Within a decade the generation covering Buenos Aires in large-format murals includes people who first held a can in that room. He never had a teacher of his own.
suggested_refs: The 'Aerosol Urbano' course at the Centro Cultural Ricardo Rojas, UBA, Avenida Corrientes
sources: ojosalcuadro.tumblr.com, 'Alfredo Segatori, un muralista de Buenos Aires' (2015)

stops.name: Villa Soldati, three facades in a month
stops.date_confidence: undated in the single source; placed by inference in the years before the Barracas commission, and the source itself was unreachable in the last pass.
stops.campa: In Villa Soldati, in the poorest south of the city, he paints three building facades twenty-five metres high inside a single month, working tenement walls in a barrio no gallery circuit visits. The scale suits him. A wall that size cannot be planned on a table; it has to be read from the pavement and answered from a swing stage, in weather, around the windows of the people who live behind it. The wall is never visible whole from anywhere he can stand while painting it.
suggested_refs: The three twenty-five-metre facades of Villa Soldati
sources: La Nacion, 'Alfredo Segatori: La pared es la primera disparadora de ideas' (nid2208090); URL returned 404 in the last pass

stops.name: Barracas, El regreso de Quinquela inaugurated
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested; the day is not recorded and is defaulted to 01. The coordinate is the Lavadero and San Antonio corner at the Riachuelo, reconciling three source descriptions of one site.
stops.campa: On the camino de sirga where Lavadero and San Antonio run down to the Riachuelo, he paints El regreso de Quinquela across a party wall a hundred metres long and thirteen high. He takes four canvases by Benito Quinquela Martin, the painter of this exact black river and its stevedores, and fuses them into a single landscape, then sets into it more than seventy portraits of the people who live on the bank. Dockworkers stand in the picture under their own faces. The river below is being dredged while he works.
suggested_refs: 'El regreso de Quinquela', camino de sirga, Barracas; the four fused canvases of Benito Quinquela Martin
sources: Turismo Buenos Aires, official page on 'El regreso de Quinquela'
Wikipedia (es), 'Alfredo Segatori', citing Perfil, Claudio Corsalini, 28 December 2014
arteforadomuseu.com.br, work listed as 'Lavadero & San Antonio'

stops.name: Barracas, the wall keeps growing
stops.date_confidence: post date of the trade-press record of the 2014 extension; the painting itself is undated within that year.
stops.campa: The wall is not finished when it is inaugurated. Through 2014 he keeps extending it along the factory building, and in December a Buenos Aires newspaper runs the headline that the largest mural in the world is being painted in Barracas. A year earlier the same brick had been called the largest in Argentina. Both descriptions are of one wall at two sizes, which is what happens to work made in public over years instead of delivered finished. Among the neighbors in the composition he paints his own son.
suggested_refs: buenosairesstreetart.com, 'Alfredo Segatori paints factory building in Barracas', 24 August 2014
sources: buenosairesstreetart.com, tag archive 'Alfredo Segatori'
Perfil, Claudio Corsalini, 'Alfredo Segatori pinta en Barracas el mural mas grande del mundo', 28 December 2014

stops.name: Barracas, two thousand square metres
stops.date_confidence: post date of the trade-press record announcing the completed work; the completion itself is undated.
stops.campa: By March 2015 the finished work covers some two thousand square metres, sprayed freehand by one man, and the city's tourism office begins calling it the largest mural in the world made by a single artist in that technique. A street-art magazine goes further and credits him with a Guinness record for it. No certificate, no date and no record number has ever been produced, and the official page beside it makes no such claim. The wall stands regardless, running longer than the block it is painted on.
suggested_refs: The unlocated Guinness assertion, made only by Street Art Latam and absent from every official source
sources: buenosairesstreetart.com, 'Alfredo Segatori paints biggest mural in the world in Buenos Aires', 17 March 2015
Turismo Buenos Aires, official page on 'El regreso de Quinquela'

stops.name: Barracas, declared of cultural interest
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested by the city tourism page; the day is not recorded and is defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Six years after it was painted, the Buenos Aires legislature declares El regreso de Quinquela of cultural interest, which turns a wall on a contaminated riverbank into heritage by vote. The camino de sirga beside it belongs to a basin sanitation plan promised for longer than the mural has existed. The declaration protects aerosol on brick standing over water that still carries a century of tanneries. He has said elsewhere, and says it again, that everything he paints is perishable and the record will outlive the paint.
suggested_refs: The Buenos Aires legislature's 2019 declaration of cultural interest for the Barracas mural
sources: Turismo Buenos Aires, official page on 'El regreso de Quinquela'
Wikipedia (es), 'Alfredo Segatori'

stops.name: New York, a named city and nothing more
stops.date_confidence: no date in any source; the stop is placed loosely among his international years and defaulted to 01 January.
stops.campa: New York appears in every account of his career and in none of them with an address. The sources name the city and stop: no borough, no wall, no photograph, no year. He paints there, and the record of it consists of the sentence saying he did. This is the ordinary fate of a trade whose product stays outdoors and whose archive is a photograph somebody may or may not have taken. He has said for years that the paint is perishable, and the record of the paint turns out to be perishable in the same way.
suggested_refs: The undocumented New York interventions, named by two sources and detailed by none
sources: Street Art Latam, 'Alfredo Segatori: el pionero que transformo el muralismo en Argentina'
La Nacion (nid2208090); URL returned 404 in the last pass

stops.name: Woodberry, Baltimore: Homo naledi on the Jones Falls
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested; the Baltimore Sun reports a three-day painting covered on 17 August 2016 and the trade-press post is dated 30 August, but the start day is not recorded.
stops.campa: On a shuttered tire factory beside the Jones Falls in Woodberry he paints for three days with the Uruguayan-born Baltimore artist Pablo Machioli. The figure they put on the brick is Homo naledi, the early human species described out of a South African cave the year before: a face barely a year old to science, painted on the wall of an industry already dead. The exchange that brings him is called Roots and Raices, pairing writers from Buenos Aires with writers from Baltimore, two port cities with the same rusted riverfront.
suggested_refs: The Roots/Raices exchange organised by Matt Fox-Tucker and Richard Best with Gallery 788, August 2016
sources: Baltimore Sun, 'Cultural exchange unites street artists from Buenos Aires and Baltimore', 17 August 2016
buenosairesstreetart.com, post of 30 August 2016

stops.name: Ciudad de Mexico, the muralists' country
stops.date_confidence: no date in any source; placed loosely within his Mexican work and defaulted to 01 January.
stops.campa: He paints in Mexico City, in the country that invented the modern political mural and produced David Alfaro Siqueiros, whose scale and whose insistence that a wall belongs to whoever walks past it he has been citing since the first reporter asked him for a lineage. What he painted there, and in what year, no source records. The visit survives as one line in a list of countries. Mexico gave him the argument he uses in Buenos Aires; his own weeks in Mexico left nothing behind that can be found.
suggested_refs: Mexican muralism as the acknowledged ancestor of his own practice
sources: Street Art Latam profile
conexionshow.com.ar, 'La Scaloneta ya tiene mural en la Ciudad'
La Nacion (nid2208090); URL returned 404 in the last pass

stops.name: Playa del Carmen, the Caribbean commissions
stops.date_confidence: no date in any source; placed loosely within the same Mexican run and defaulted.
stops.campa: On the Caribbean coast of Quintana Roo he works Playa del Carmen, a resort town whose walls are painted for visitors rather than for neighbors, which inverts everything his method assumes. In Buenos Aires he asks the owner and then answers to the barrio. Here the wall faces an economy of arrivals. No source names the building or the year, and no photograph of the work has surfaced in anything reachable; the town survives in his record as one more place-name on a list of stops.
suggested_refs: The undocumented Quintana Roo commissions
sources: La Nacion (nid2208090); URL returned 404 in the last pass

stops.name: Cancun, the last of the Mexican list
stops.date_confidence: no date in any source; placed loosely and defaulted.
stops.campa: Cancun closes the Mexican run in the accounts, named beside Playa del Carmen and the capital with the same total absence of detail. No wall, no commissioner, no year. He is by now a muralist whose Argentine work is inventoried post by dated post in the trade press while his foreign work vanishes into a subordinate clause. Nothing followed him to Quintana Roo that kept a record. What is left of the Mexican months is four city names in a biography written by other people.
suggested_refs: The Cancun stop, attested only as a place-name
sources: conexionshow.com.ar, 'La Scaloneta ya tiene mural en la Ciudad'

stops.name: Anden 2222, the recyclers' atelier
stops.date_confidence: undated in the single source, described as ongoing; placed by inference before the Palermo metal works. The source URL returned 404 in the last pass.
stops.campa: He works out of an atelier at Anden 2222, tied to the Cooperativa de Recicladores Urbanos El Ceibo, whose members go through the city's discards for a living. Their salvage becomes his material: bumpers, exhaust pipes, sheet steel, the parts of cars that outlive the cars. The foundation he chairs takes the same name as the address. With paint he covered walls; with scrap he assembles them, and his palette is whatever the neighborhood threw out that week.
suggested_refs: The Fundacion Cultural Anden 2222 and the Cooperativa El Ceibo, founding year unrecorded
sources: La Nacion (nid2208090); URL returned 404 in the last pass
arteforadomuseu.com.br, biography page for 'Pelado'

stops.name: Gorriti and Lavalleja, Palermo: El viejo del desarmadero
stops.date_confidence: no source gives a year of making; Wikipedia records only that it stood among the city's most-visited works in 2017, which places the making at or before that year. Month and day unknown.
stops.campa: On the corner of Gorriti and Lavalleja, out of a scrapyard's bumpers and exhaust pipes and cast-off metal, he builds an old man. The figure is anonymous, enormous, and assembled entirely from what the neighborhood has already scrapped. People come to photograph it, and by 2017 it is counted among the most-visited artworks on the street in Buenos Aires. He listens to what the visitors say and lets their readings reshape the thing. Of everything he hears, one description is the one he keeps.
stops.quote: Lo que más me gustó de todo lo que escuché es que se parecía a un dios desorientado
stops.quote_source: Alfredo Segatori, interviewed by Hernán Firpo, Clarín, 23 December 2017 (quoted verbatim in the Spanish Wikipedia article; the Clarín page itself was blocked)
suggested_refs: 'El viejo del desarmadero', Gorriti y Lavalleja, Palermo, year of making unrecorded
sources: Wikipedia (es), 'Alfredo Segatori'
Clarin, Hernan Firpo, 'Entrevista Alfredo Segatori: el primer y mas groso muralista urbano', 23 December 2017

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the method stated aloud
stops.date_confidence: publication date of the interview, attested.
stops.campa: A newspaper bills him at the end of 2017 as the first and biggest urban muralist in the country, then asks him how he works. He answers with four verbs and no theory whatsoever. He wants rough walls rather than smooth ones, because a surface already weathered and patched takes the paint and gives something back. Twenty years after the first wall he is still scraping them himself, which is the part of the trade nobody photographs and the part he has never handed to anybody else.
stops.quote: ver una pared, pedir permiso, rasquetearla y trabajarla
stops.quote_source: Alfredo Segatori, interviewed by Hernán Firpo, Clarín, 23 December 2017 (quoted verbatim in the Spanish Wikipedia article; the Clarín page itself was blocked)
suggested_refs: The four-verb method: see a wall, ask permission, scrape it, work it
sources: Clarin, Hernan Firpo, 23 December 2017
Wikipedia (es), 'Alfredo Segatori'

stops.name: Hipodromo Argentino de Palermo, Lunatica Arte and Turf
stops.date_confidence: reported for 2018 in the research record but absent from the retrieved text of the cited profile; unverified, and the month and day are unknown. The weakest item retained in this file.
stops.campa: At the racetrack in Palermo he puts together an event called Lunatica Arte and Turf and gathers, by the account that survives, more than four hundred and fifty artists onto the grounds. For once he is not the man on the wall but the man assembling the bill. The role follows the same instinct as the metal works: take what is scattered across the city, bring it to one address, and let people walk through it. The racetrack crowd and the mural crowd do not ordinarily stand on the same grass.
suggested_refs: 'Lunatica Arte & Turf' at the Hipodromo Argentino de Palermo, unverified in the cited source
sources: Diario Contexto, 'Alfredo Segatori y los colores de la identidad popular' (event not found in the retrieved text)

stops.name: Humboldt and Cabrera, Palermo: the front of La Covacha
stops.date_confidence: post date of the trade-press record; the work itself is undated within 2018.
stops.campa: He faces a Palermo bar called La Covacha entirely in recovered material, so that the front of the building becomes a sculpture built from what the barrio no longer wants. It is a paid commission and it is made of garbage, and he treats that as no contradiction at all. The metal arrives through the same channel as everything else he assembles in these years: the recyclers, the scrapyards, the cooperative. The building keeps a front that a scrapyard would otherwise have sold by weight.
suggested_refs: The recycled-material facade of La Covacha, Humboldt y Cabrera, Palermo
sources: buenosairesstreetart.com, tag archive 'Alfredo Segatori', post of 6 December 2018

stops.name: Darsena F, Puerto Nuevo: Fauna Portuaria
stops.date_confidence: date, size and address attested in the Spanish Wikipedia text; the coordinate is approximate because direct geocoding of Darsena F failed. The Infobae article behind the entry returns 404.
stops.campa: On Avenida Rafael Obligado, at the sand basin of Puerto Nuevo, he inaugurates Fauna Portuaria on the longest day of the southern year: twelve hundred square metres of native Argentine animals painted across the walls of a working aggregate port. Jaguars, llamas, condors, macaws, a puma, hummingbirds. The species the country is losing go up on the machinery of loading and unloading, at the exact place where the river is dredged for sand. Trucks pass under the condor all day long.
suggested_refs: 'Fauna Portuaria', Avenida Rafael Obligado y calle 1, Darsena F, the sand port of Puerto Nuevo
sources: Wikipedia (es), 'Alfredo Segatori', citing Infobae, 23 December 2018 (cited URL returns 404)

stops.name: Puerto Arenero, the Agrecom silos
stops.date_confidence: publication date of the Perfil report, fetched directly; the painting itself is undated within 2019 and the coordinate is the approximate port position.
stops.campa: The third edition of his Exabrupto de Color goes up on the Agrecom silos in the sand sector of the port, among the largest structures on that waterfront. For this one he puts the can down: exterior latex, paint machines, compressors, the tools of industrial painting turned against an industrial object. The colour arrives in quantity rather than by hand. Asked what remains of work made at this size on somebody else's silo, he answers without any apparent regret.
stops.quote: esto es arte perecedero y lo que queda básicamente son los registros fotográficos y de video
stops.quote_source: Alfredo Segatori, quoted by César Calvo, 'La explosión de color en el puerto de Buenos Aires continúa', Perfil, 13 September 2019 (primary source fetched directly)
suggested_refs: The Agrecom silos of the Puerto Arenero, third edition of 'Exabrupto de Color'
sources: Perfil, Cesar Calvo, 'La explosion de color en el puerto de Buenos Aires continua', 13 September 2019

stops.name: Playa Brava, Punta del Este: the hand repainted
stops.date_confidence: publication date of the report; the intervention is dated only to January 2020, and the coordinate is approximate because geocoding of the sculpture failed. The Bacanal source failed DNS resolution in the last pass.
stops.campa: The Exabrupto de Color crosses the Plata to Punta del Este in the first days of 2020 and lands on the most photographed object in Uruguay: the five concrete fingers of Mario Irarrázabal's La Mano, rising out of the sand at Playa Brava. He colours the hand. Several other city spaces go the same way, on an initiative driven by a producer and a businessman rather than by any government. It is the last summer before the borders close, and the hand keeps his colour for as long as the salt and the sun allow.
suggested_refs: Mario Irarrazabal's 'La Mano' at Playa Brava, coloured for the Uruguayan edition of Exabrupto de Color
sources: Bacanal, 'El exabrupto de color llega a Punta del Este', 2 January 2020 (site failed DNS resolution; known through the Wikipedia citation)

stops.name: Rio Gallegos, the Patagonian stop
stops.date_confidence: no date in any source; placed loosely among his Argentine travels and defaulted. The single source URL returned 404 in the last pass.
stops.campa: He paints in Río Gallegos, on the estuary in Santa Cruz, more than two thousand kilometres south of the Riachuelo, in a wind that decides by itself how any outdoor work gets done down there. The source recording the visit names the town and nothing else: no wall, no subject, no year. It is one of the hundred-odd works credited to him across the country, and most of them survive in the record in exactly this condition: a town name with nothing under it.
suggested_refs: The Rio Gallegos intervention, attested only as a place-name
sources: La Nacion, 'Alfredo Segatori: La pared es la primera disparadora de ideas' (nid2208090); URL returned 404 in the last pass

stops.name: Puerto Esperanza, Misiones: the red-earth north
stops.date_confidence: no date in any source; placed loosely and defaulted. The single source URL returned 404 in the last pass.
stops.campa: On the Paraná above Iguazú he paints in Puerto Esperanza, a timber town in Misiones that looks nothing like Buenos Aires and has no muralists of its own. Again the record consists of the name of the town. He goes where a wall is offered, and walls are offered in places that have no press to photograph the result. In most corners of the country the record of what he painted is held by the people who stood in the street and watched him make it, and by nobody else.
suggested_refs: The Puerto Esperanza intervention, attested only as a place-name
sources: La Nacion (nid2208090); URL returned 404 in the last pass

stops.name: Miranda 4778, Monte Castro: Mirando Miranda
stops.date_confidence: post date of the trade-press record documenting the finished giraffe; the painting itself is undated within 2019.
stops.campa: On an eleven-storey building on calle Miranda he paints a giraffe the full height of the facade, its neck craning up past the balconies of people who now live inside the animal. He calls it Mirando Miranda, looking at Miranda, which is the street and also what the giraffe is doing. Monte Castro has no coastline, no zoo, and no reason whatever for a giraffe. It gets one anyway, visible from four blocks off, and the building acquires a name in the barrio that has nothing to do with its address.
suggested_refs: 'Mirando Miranda', Miranda 4778, Monte Castro
sources: Diario Contexto, 'Alfredo Segatori y los colores de la identidad popular'

stops.name: Aristobulo del Valle 50, La Boca: San Diego de la Boca
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day not recorded and defaulted to 01 January; the coordinate is approximate, derived from the street's run rather than a successful address geocode.
stops.campa: Diego Maradona dies in November 2020, and in the barrio that claims him hardest Segatori paints San Diego de la Boca, a few streets up from Caminito. The title does the work: not a footballer, a local saint, canonised by the neighborhood that watched him play at fifteen. The city fills with Maradona murals that season, hundreds of them, painted by everybody who owns a can. This one goes up in a barrio of corrugated iron and paint where sanctity and football have never been kept in separate rooms.
suggested_refs: 'San Diego de la Boca', Aristobulo del Valle 50, painted after Maradona's death on 25 November 2020
sources: Wikipedia (es), 'Alfredo Segatori', citing Perfil

stops.name: San Francisco, Cordoba: La vaca que se fue volando
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not recorded and defaulted to 01 January.
stops.campa: He paints grain silos in San Francisco, in the dairy country of eastern Córdoba, and puts on them a cow that has flown away. La vaca que se fue volando stands over the province's own product, on the towers where the harvest waits for the truck. Away from the port and the tenement wall he works the way he always has: he takes the working object of the place, puts the animal of the place on it, and paints it at a size a driver can read from the highway.
suggested_refs: 'La vaca que se fue volando' on the grain silos of San Francisco, Cordoba
sources: Wikipedia (es), 'Alfredo Segatori'
Infonegocios San Francisco, 'En San Francisco en las paredes hablan y las vacas vuelan'

stops.name: Villa del Parque, Panda Pandemial
stops.date_confidence: publication date of the record documenting the finished work; the painting itself is undated within 2022.
stops.campa: Ten storeys of party wall in Villa del Parque take a panda scaled to the tower, painted in the long tail of the pandemic and named after it. The city's mural trade has moved onto residential high-rises by now, single enormous figures facing the street from buildings full of people who did not commission them and mostly like them anyway. He works these the way he worked Soldati a decade before: from a stage, freehand, deciding a face at a distance he cannot step back to.
suggested_refs: 'Panda Pandemial', ten-storey party wall, Villa del Parque
sources: muralesbuenosaires.com.ar, 'Panda Pandemial', 17 June 2022
Wikipedia (es), 'Alfredo Segatori'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, La Scaloneta on a staircase
stops.date_confidence: no date beyond the months following the December 2022 World Cup; defaulted to 01 December, and the source names no street or corner, so the canonical city pin is used.
stops.campa: After Argentina wins the World Cup he paints a public staircase for the squad, and the city calls the work La Scaloneta, after the coach whose surname the whole country has turned into a vehicle. Which staircase, in which barrio, the record does not say. The nation is painting itself that summer in a way it has not done in decades, and he is inside that wave: a man who has argued for thirty years that a wall belongs to whoever walks past it, working in the month everyone agrees with him.

stops.name: Parque Chacabuco, Dino Rex on a skateboard
stops.date_confidence: post date of the trade-press record; the painting itself is undated within 2023.
stops.campa: Two dinosaurs go up in Parque Chacabuco on a freehand aerosol pass. One is a tyrannosaurus on a skateboard wearing a cap backwards with the number ten on it, which in this country names one man and only one. He calls it Dino Rex. The barrio has skate ramps rather than a stadium, and the joke is built for the children who use them: the oldest predator on earth, wearing a borrowed shirt number, riding a board through a public park in the west of the city.
suggested_refs: 'Dino Rex', Parque Chacabuco, the number ten as a Maradona reference

stops.name: Floresta, the sculptor and the son
stops.date_confidence: no source dates the marriage or the son's birth; placed loosely and defaulted. Two accounts name the son differently, Mateo in a 2015 interview and Theo in the city's page on the Barracas mural, and nothing decides between them.
stops.campa: He marries the sculptor Paula Pons. Their son draws early, and his father paints him into the Barracas wall among the dockworkers, a child's face set inside a landscape borrowed from a dead painter of the same river. Two accounts of the family give the boy different names, Mateo in one interview and Theo in another, and nothing decides between them. She works in three dimensions and he works on brick. No source dates the marriage or the boy's birth.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, BADA, direct from the artists
stops.date_confidence: undated in the source, which names the participation without a year or a venue; placed loosely and defaulted. An earlier gloss calling BADA a design biennial in Recoleta was wrong and is discarded.
stops.campa: He takes part in BADA, Buenos Aires Directo de Artistas, a fair built on the principle that work is sold by the person who made it with no dealer standing in between. The premise suits a man whose whole career has consisted of dealing directly with whoever owns the wall. Neither the venue nor the year survives in the account. What survives is the fact of the participation, which puts the muralist indoors for a weekend, at a table, sitting beside his own portable work.

stops.name: Caminito, La Boca 5.0
stops.date_confidence: undated in the source, described only as recent; placed loosely and defaulted.
stops.campa: With the operators of Caminito he develops La Boca 5.0, an immersive experience laid over the most visited three hundred metres in Argentina. The corrugated houses of Caminito were coloured in the first place by Benito Quinquela Martín, whose four canvases he had already fused into two thousand square metres of wall further up the same river. He returns to the barrio working in staged experience rather than pigment, on ground that has been a painter's invention since long before he was born.
suggested_refs: 'La Boca 5.0', developed with Visit Caminito
sources: Diario Contexto, 'Alfredo Segatori y los colores de la identidad popular'

stops.name: Miami, the exabrupto abroad
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the month is unrecorded and the event itself is contested between two differently branded Martin Fierro ceremonies, so no award is named here.
stops.campa: He turns up in Miami around a Martín Fierro awards night and stages a party out of his own aesthetic: recovered material, colour applied by the bucket, a room assembled from the exabrupto. The same period ties him to work referencing Inter Miami, the club that has just acquired the most watched footballer alive. Florida is where Argentine celebrity keeps its second house, and the muralist of the Riachuelo arrives there as a producer of atmosphere rather than as a man on a swing stage.

stops.name: La Boca, Galeria Social Rimini and Il Piccolo Vapore
stops.date_confidence: the source gives an opening date of 23 August without naming a year; the year here is inferred and uncertain.
stops.campa: He takes part in reopening the Galería Social Rimini and the Il Piccolo Vapore space in La Boca, folding a gallery and a neighborhood project into one address. La Boca has become his base of operations, and it is not the barrio he came from. Floresta made him. La Boca holds him now, a barrio of Italian surnames and ironwork on a black river, worked by painters for a century before he arrived with a compressor and a scraper. The year of the reopening is not recorded.

stops.name: Palermo, Gardel and Charly Garcia on two walls
stops.date_confidence: post date of the trade-press record; no street address is given in the source, so the coordinate is a general Palermo placement.
stops.campa: In December he adds two faces to Palermo: Carlos Gardel, who fixed what the country sounds like when it is sad, and Charly García, who put the same country through an amplifier. Tango and rock go up on the barrio walls he has been painting since he built an old man out of car parts a few blocks from here. No street address survives for either wall in the record of that month. Palermo carries a run of his portraits by now, added one at a time over years, each face picked by him rather than requested.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, more than a hundred walls
stops.date_confidence: a standing summary rather than a dated event; the works total is undated in the sources and the date marks the last research pass, when his own domain was observed suspended.
stops.campa: Over thirty years he paints more than a hundred works across Argentina, and by his own account nearly all of them are already dying. Rain takes them, owners repaint them, buildings come down. He chairs a foundation named after a railway platform, teaches the can to strangers, and states his whole trajectory in one line on a phone screen. The website carrying his own archive goes dark in 2026, suspended, which is precisely the fate he has been describing to interviewers for a decade.
